stories.headline: Trump suggests calling the Strait of Hormuz 'Trump Strait'
stories.dek: President Donald Trump on Wednesday floated a new name for the Strait of Hormuz in a Truth Social post during ongoing clashes with Iran.
stories.body:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday floated a new name for the Strait of Hormuz in a Truth Social post during ongoing clashes with Iran.

"Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be 'hotter' than ever before!" Trump wrote. SCMP said Trump later implied he was not serious.

The Hindu and SCMP both said Trump has recently threatened to claim sovereignty over the waterway and posted a map showing it as a "new U.S. territory." The Hindu said the idea followed other name changes by Trump, including renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" and ordering Lake Ontario renamed "Lake America."

The suggestion came as fighting and attacks continued around the strait. The Hindu said Iran has effectively shut down the chokepoint and that U.S. forces launched fresh strikes near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday after what Trump said were new Iranian minelaying efforts. The New York Times reported that two more oil tankers were attacked near Oman on Monday and that oil prices rose more than 2 percent. The Hindu said about a fifth of the world's oil passes through the strait.
stories.so_what: Because about a fifth of the world's oil passes through the strait, attacks and disruption there can quickly push up oil prices.

stories.headline: US strike hits wedding gathering in southern Iranian town, reports say
stories.dek: A U.S. missile hit a home in the southern Iranian town of Kuhestak on Tuesday where dozens of people had gathered for the wedding of a fisherman's daughter, according to a rights…
stories.body:
A U.S. missile hit a home in the southern Iranian town of Kuhestak on Tuesday where dozens of people had gathered for the wedding of a fisherman's daughter, according to a rights group and Iranian media. Heavy explosions shook the coastal town on the Strait of Hormuz, and security footage carried by Iran's semi-official Fars news agency showed fireballs lighting up the night sky.

Accounts of the toll differed. Iranian state media, cited by the South China Morning Post, said four people were killed - two women and two children - and more than 60 were wounded. The New York Times reported that Iranian authorities said five people were killed and 67 others were wounded. The rights group cited by SCMP said one of the children, a teenager, was killed in another strike on a nearby communications tower.

The New York Times said a weapons expert and a visual analysis by the newspaper found that the bomb that hit the residential area was American. The strike came during the latest round of American bombardment in southern Iran that the U.S. military said was targeting air defences, radar systems and maritime assets.

U.S. Central Command spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins said the U.S. military was looking into the reports of the strike on a wedding. He did not say whether the military had opened a formal investigation, according to SCMP.
stories.so_what: The reported civilian deaths and injuries add to the risks for people living near the Strait of Hormuz as U.S. attacks continue in southern Iran.
stories.what_now: U.S. Central Command spokesman Captain Tim Hawkins said the military was looking into the reports of the strike.

stories.headline: Carney tells Trump officials to stop ‘throwing shade’ in trade dispute
stories.dek: Prime Minister Mark Carney told Trump administration officials to stop using taunts as Canada and the United States remain locked in a trade war.
stories.body:
Prime Minister Mark Carney told Trump administration officials to stop using taunts as Canada and the United States remain locked in a trade war. Sky News quoted Carney as saying: "Stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, and stop trying to be tough."

The New York Times reported the remarks came amid the trade conflict between the two countries. It said Canada’s Liberals swept three special votes.

The New York Times also reported that new polling suggested strong support for Carney and for his retaliatory tariffs against the United States. Sky’s report framed Carney’s comments as a direct message to President Donald Trump’s officials.

Neither source in the material provided detailed the setting for Carney’s remarks or identified which U.S. officials he was addressing. Both sources described the exchange as part of the broader Canada-U.S. trade talks and dispute.
stories.so_what: The episode shows Carney is pairing hardline trade rhetoric with political momentum at home, a combination that could affect how far Canada goes in its standoff with the United States.

stories.headline: Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigns amid clash over Army changes
stories.dek: U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down, according to a Department of Defense official cited by Axios, and Sky News reported the White House announced his departure.
stories.body:
U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down, according to a Department of Defense official cited by Axios, and Sky News reported the White House announced his departure. Axios said the resignation was announced Monday and that Driscoll is expected to leave the Pentagon in the coming days, citing The Wall Street Journal.

Axios reported two key reasons for the resignation: Driscoll felt his modernization initiatives were being blocked, and he was reacting to the chaos created by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's firing of senior generals. Axios also reported Driscoll recently spoke with President Donald Trump to express concerns about the state of the Army, and that a White House official said he had been asked to stay until after the midterms but said it was time for him to go.

Axios described an icy relationship between Driscoll and Hegseth. It said some U.S. officials described Hegseth as "suspicious and paranoid" toward Driscoll, partly because of Driscoll's close relationship with Vice President JD Vance, his Yale Law classmate. Axios also cited The New York Times as reporting that tension included a dispute over four officers on a promotions list, and Fox News as reporting that Driscoll resisted pressure from Hegseth to fire senior adviser Col. David Butler.

White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said Driscoll had been "highly effective in advancing President Trump's agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army" and credited him with leadership during military operations, restoring readiness and lethality, and assisting with Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Axios said Driscoll was the youngest Army secretary in U.S. history and oversaw an annual budget and a workforce of more than 1 million active-duty, National Guard and reserve soldiers, plus more than 330,000 civilian employees.
stories.so_what: The Army, the military's largest service, is left without Senate-confirmed civilian or uniformed leadership, Axios reported.
stories.what_now: Axios reported Driscoll is expected to leave the Pentagon in the coming days, and a White House official said he had been asked to stay until after the midterms.

stories.headline: Xi visits Egypt as China and Egypt deepen ties amid regional war
stories.dek: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Cairo on Tuesday evening for a three-day visit and held talks Wednesday with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi.
stories.body:
Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Cairo on Tuesday evening for a three-day visit and held talks Wednesday with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi. It is Xi’s first visit to Egypt in a decade and his first trip to the region since visiting Saudi Arabia in 2022, according to NPR and The Hindu.

According to China’s state-run Xinhua news agency, Xi said Cairo and Beijing should jointly oppose what he called "unilateralism and acts of bullying" and should "work together for a more just and equitable global governance system." The leaders also marked 70 years of diplomatic ties with opinion pieces in Egypt’s state-run newspapers. Xi wrote that the two countries should "expand the scope of pragmatic collaboration" through development, while el-Sissi praised Chinese investment and reiterated Cairo’s support for China’s claim that Taiwan is part of its territory.

NPR and The Hindu said Egypt sees closer ties with China as a way to diversify its strategic partnerships. The reports said China has invested more than $10 billion in Egypt, including a business hub east of Cairo and an electric rail line for industry in the Nile Delta. Annual trade between China and Egypt is estimated at $20 billion, compared with $15.7 billion in trade between the United States and Egypt in 2025.

The visit comes during the war with Iran and after China and Egypt held a multiday air exercise across Egypt in August, the first-ever combat exercise for China’s J-16 fighter jets and Egypt’s French-made Rafale fighters, the reports said. NPR and The Hindu said oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have been heavily disrupted by the Iran war, making Egypt’s Suez Canal an important alternative route for energy supplies out of the region.
stories.so_what: For ordinary readers, the visit signals that Egypt is building stronger ties with both Washington and Beijing at a time when war is disrupting trade and energy routes in the region.
stories.what_now: The Hindu reported Xi will be in Egypt for three days.

stories.headline: Zack Polanski seeks Green nomination for Holborn and St Pancras byelection
stories.dek: Zack Polanski, the Green party leader in England and Wales, said he intends to run in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection after Keir Starmer resigned as MP for the seat.
stories.body:
Zack Polanski, the Green party leader in England and Wales, said he intends to run in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection after Keir Starmer resigned as MP for the seat. The BBC said Polanski plans to run in the former prime minister's seat, and the Guardian reported on Thursday that he had announced he would seek to stand.

The Guardian reported that local Green party members support Polanski running and that no clear local activist with significant support is expected to oppose him. Polanski campaigned in the Holborn area on Tuesday with fellow Green MP Hannah Spencer, according to the Guardian. He told the Camden New Journal he would "stand up for people struggling to pay their bills" if elected, and said separately that the contest would be a "referendum on ending rip-off Britain".

The seat became vacant when Starmer announced he was standing down as an MP, according to the Guardian. The Guardian said the move carries risk because the constituency has traditionally been considered safe for Labour.

Labour is also preparing to choose a candidate. The Guardian reported that the party will not use an all-women shortlist and plans to announce its candidate by next Wednesday, with applications closing on Friday and shortlisting expected by the start of next week. It said Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of Camden council, is seen as the frontrunner, while Adam Hug, Nash Ali and Rishi Madlani have also been mentioned.
stories.so_what: The contest will test whether the Greens can turn higher-profile national leadership into support in a seat Labour has long been expected to hold.
stories.what_now: Green nominations are expected to open soon, with the party due to select its candidate by the end of next week, while Labour says it will announce its candidate by next Wednesday.

stories.headline: Iran Red Crescent asks ICC to investigate US strike on wedding party
stories.dek: The Iranian Red Crescent Society said it asked the International Criminal Court on Wednesday to investigate a United States missile strike that hit a wedding party in Kuhestak, a…
stories.body:
The Iranian Red Crescent Society said it asked the International Criminal Court on Wednesday to investigate a United States missile strike that hit a wedding party in Kuhestak, a town in southern Iran. The group said the attack happened at 9:30pm local time on Tuesday and called for "an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation" because of the "civilian character of the location".

The Red Crescent said at least four people were killed and 67 were wounded. It said the dead were two women and two children, aged four and 16, and warned the death toll could rise because some of the injured are in critical condition. An Iranian official, cited by Al Jazeera, said most of the wounded were also women and children.

The Red Crescent said the strike could amount to a "war crime" under international law. Iran's envoy to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, also urged the UN Security Council to denounce what he called a "horrific and appalling crime" and said the deliberate targeting and killing of civilians, including children, amounts to a war crime.

U.S. Central Command said it was aware of Iranian media reports about the attack, but said it does not target civilians. CBS reported the U.S.-Iran war had ramped back up as the two sides traded strikes and President Donald Trump downplayed the idea of a peace deal. Al Jazeera reported Iran's Health Ministry said at least 18 people were killed and 142 wounded in Tuesday's strikes overall.
stories.so_what: The ICC request adds legal pressure over civilian deaths, even though neither the United States nor Iran is automatically under the court's jurisdiction.

stories.headline: Sources split on Russia-Ukraine war path as strikes intensify
stories.dek: The New York Times reports that Russia and Ukraine are each using missiles and drones to try to pound the other into giving up.
stories.body:
The New York Times reports that Russia and Ukraine are each using missiles and drones to try to pound the other into giving up. It says the fighting is producing ceaseless human suffering.

The paper says there is no sign that either country's determination will weaken. It describes the conflict as an escalating spiral with no end in sight.

The Hindu, in an editorial on the conflict, takes a different approach. It says Russia must opt for diplomatic engagement with the West and warns, in its headline, not to gamble on the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The two sources do not provide a shared new event, date or casualty count. But together they portray a war still driven by attacks and by competing arguments over whether escalation or diplomacy will shape what comes next.
stories.so_what: For ordinary readers, the reports point to a war that is still causing suffering and offers no clear sign of easing soon.

stories.headline: Germany blames Russia for attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport
stories.dek: Germany said on Tuesday that it holds Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4.
stories.body:
Germany said on Tuesday that it holds Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 4. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said at a press conference in Berlin that police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiated Russian responsibility. The New York Times said Germany accused Moscow weeks after an explosive-laden drone was found near a Ukrainian plane at a German airport last month.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems were known from other Russian hybrid operations and Russia's war against Ukraine. German authorities said they found a drone fitted with explosives and a detonation mechanism in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport between Ukrainian cargo aircraft on the evening of August 4. DW reported that investigators also believe a second drone may have collided with a DHL aircraft nearby, and that German media last week reported a third explosive-laden drone was also discovered at the airport.

Dobrindt called the incident a hybrid attack and said Germany was not at war but was a daily target of hybrid warfare. Wadephul said Germany would coordinate its response with European Union and NATO partners. He said Germany was tightening entry controls for Russian nationals, would propose listing more Russian individuals for EU sanctions, had summoned the Russian ambassador in Berlin, would close the Russian consulate in Bonn from September 18 and would rescind a contract enabling the operation of the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said NATO stood in full solidarity with Germany after what he called the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Germany had taken strong measures and that hybrid attacks would not go without a clear response. Russia denied the accusation. DW reported that President Vladimir Putin said Germany's leadership was trying to deflect from its own failings and claimed the proof had been planted, while the New York Times said he called the accusation "a grave mistake."
stories.so_what: The case points to a direct security threat at a major German transport and logistics hub and is prompting new restrictions and diplomatic measures that could affect travel and relations with Russia.
stories.what_now: Germany said it will close the Russian consulate in Bonn from September 18.

stories.headline: Vance tells Jewish Republicans Israel is key to U.S. security
stories.dek: Vice President JD Vance appeared Monday before the Republican Jewish Coalition at the Venetian hotel in Las Vegas, where he called Israel "extremely important to America's…
stories.body:
Vice President JD Vance appeared Monday before the Republican Jewish Coalition at the Venetian hotel in Las Vegas, where he called Israel "extremely important to America's national security" and condemned rising antisemitism, according to two sources familiar with his remarks cited by Axios.

Axios reported that during a 30-minute Q&A with former Minnesota Sen. Norm Coleman, Vance said "Jew hatred is corrosive to the soul" and blamed some of the recent rise in antisemitism on immigration. He said "a lot" of it was "coming from these Third World immigrants importing these ancient ethnic hatreds" and added, "If you want to bring ethnic hatreds with you, don't bother coming to the United States."

The appearance came after months of tension with pro-Israel conservatives over Vance's comments about Israel and Iran, according to Axios. Axios said Jewish Republicans have also long expressed discomfort over Vance's relationship with Tucker Carlson, who has faced accusations of antisemitism. When asked how Republicans should deal with right-of-center podcasters critical of Israel, including Carlson, Joe Rogan, Megyn Kelly and Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes, Axios reported that Vance said Republicans should aggressively engage them and make the case for Israel.

Politico reported that Vance's answer to a question about Carlson left some in the audience disappointed. Axios said Vance did not address his relationship with Carlson, but defended Rogan and criticized Fuentes, saying Fuentes "has nothing but hate in his heart."
stories.so_what: The speech showed Vance trying to shore up support with a skeptical Republican constituency as he is expected to prepare for a 2028 presidential run, according to Axios.

stories.headline: Chevron and Eni sign deals to expand oil projects in Venezuela
stories.dek: Chevron and several other energy companies signed multibillion-dollar deals in Caracas on Wednesday to expand oil and energy projects in Venezuela.
stories.body:
Chevron and several other energy companies signed multibillion-dollar deals in Caracas on Wednesday to expand oil and energy projects in Venezuela. The ceremony was overseen by interim President Delcy Rodriguez and U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright, according to Al Jazeera, while NPR reported Wright appeared at Miraflores Palace alongside Chevron CEO Mike Wirth and Rodriguez.

Chevron said it will expand existing operations in Venezuela as part of a joint venture and invest over $7 billion over the next five years. NPR said the company plans to raise production to about 600,000 barrels of oil per day. Al Jazeera reported Chevron's deal covers two additional oil fields in the Orinoco Belt and that output from the project will more than double in five years.

Al Jazeera reported Italy's Eni said it gained exclusive rights to explore the giant Junin 5 oilfield, and GE Vernova will help repair Venezuela's electricity grid. Wright said the deals with Chevron, GE Vernova and Eni were "critical in starting this ball rolling of peace, opportunity, and prosperity" in the country. Wirth called Chevron's agreement "an important milestone for Chevron, our partners, and the Venezuelan people."

The deals come days after Washington and Caracas announced a separate agreement giving the U.S. access to 17 Venezuelan oil fields. NPR said those fields are estimated at 65 billion barrels of oil. Al Jazeera said the 17 fields represent about a fifth of Venezuela's total reserves and reported Wright said Venezuela's total oil output could rise to 2 million barrels per day by the end of the decade, from 1.25 million barrels per day today.
stories.so_what: The agreements could affect oil supply and prices over time, but the sources say Venezuela will still need major investment and repairs to raise production substantially.

stories.headline: Uber cuts about 10% of workforce in global restructuring
stories.dek: Uber said on Wednesday it is laying off about 10% of its workforce worldwide as part of what CEO Dara Khosrowshahi called significant organizational changes.
stories.body:
Uber said on Wednesday it is laying off about 10% of its workforce worldwide as part of what CEO Dara Khosrowshahi called significant organizational changes. The Hindu, citing a recent SEC filing, said Uber has roughly 34,000 employees, while TechCrunch said the cuts amount to about 3,300 people, or about 10% of global headcount.

In a message to employees released Wednesday, Khosrowshahi said Uber had grown more complex, with more layers, more coordination and more fragmented ownership. He said the company was making the platform "simpler and faster," adding that "a leaner organization will mean clearer ownership, faster decisions, and more time spent building rather than coordinating."

TechCrunch reported the restructuring will shrink the number of managers by 20%, cut the number of one- and two-person teams by 50%, and move some managers into individual contributor roles. It also said, citing Bloomberg's reporting, that Uber is letting go staff who are more than seven layers down from the CEO. Both sources said Uber is consolidating parts of its delivery business, and both said the company will allow less than or only around 1% of employees to work remotely.

The Hindu said Uber was also shutting down its business in Nigeria and Uganda on Wednesday, after leaving Tanzania earlier this year. It said Wedbush Securities expects Uber to save around $1.75 billion through the layoffs and invest that into growth areas. The Hindu also reported Uber shares were up more than 2.5% in midday trading.
stories.so_what: The changes could affect Uber workers across many countries and signal a broader push by the company to centralize jobs in key hubs including New York and San Francisco.

stories.headline: Dutch central bank shifts 86 metric tons of gold to London
stories.dek: The Dutch central bank, DNB, said it moved about 86 metric tons of gold from New York and Ottawa to London between March and August.
stories.body:
The Dutch central bank, DNB, said it moved about 86 metric tons of gold from New York and Ottawa to London between March and August. DNB said the transfer was made because of increasing geopolitical unrest and to strengthen its crisis preparedness.

DNB said gold stored with the Bank of England is recognized as the world's most easily tradable gold because it meets international trade standards. It said bullion held in the U.S. and Canada could not be used as quickly and directly in a crisis. DNB Governor Olaf Sleijpen said, "With this relocation, we have improved the tradability of our gold reserves. We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness."

After the move, DNB said London holds 32.1% of its gold reserves, while its cash center in Zeist in the Netherlands holds 30.8%. New York and Ottawa now hold 18.5% each, according to DNB.

CNBC said the move comes as gold prices have surged and after France replaced 129 metric tons of gold held in New York with bullion bought in Europe between July 2025 and January 2026. BBC also reported that the Dutch central bank removed some of its gold reserves from the U.S. and Canada, citing increasing geopolitical unrest.

A spokesperson told the BBC the listing was not "live" on the site across the two months it was present, so "some of our automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the closed listing". stories.headline: Trump administration backs OpenAI in New York Times copyright suit
stories.dek: The Trump administration has sided with OpenAI in its copyright fight with The New York Times, which sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 over the use of its articles to train AI…
stories.body:
The Trump administration has sided with OpenAI in its copyright fight with The New York Times, which sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 over the use of its articles to train AI systems. In a brief filed in Manhattan federal court on Tuesday, the Justice Department said the United States has a "strong interest" in whether AI training on copyrighted works is considered fair use because it affects whether the country can "retain global leadership in artificial intelligence."

The filing said training large language models on internet writings is protected by fair use, calling AI training "extraordinarily transformative" and arguing that the "creative possibilities and public benefits" "far outweigh any competitive harm." Government lawyers wrote that siding with the Times and other publishers would thwart "creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility." The Hindu said the department also tied that argument to national security, saying AI models can help officials analyse and draw inferences from real-world facts.

The New York Times said on Wednesday that the administration "is siding with a handful of trillion-dollar AI companies at the expense of the countless American creators whose work they stole." Spokesperson Graham James said, "Both AI and creators can thrive - AI companies simply need to pay fairly for the content that makes their products possible, as copyright law requires." Wired also reported criticism from the Authors Guild, whose chief executive Mary Rasenberger called the government's letter "replete with faulty arguments and a gross misunderstanding of the fair use doctrine and copyright law."

The case is one of many lawsuits over whether AI companies can train tools on copyrighted material without permission. The Guardian reported this is the first time the US government has weighed in on the broader AI copyright fight, while Wired said the administration noted its arguments apply to this case and related cases involving other publishers and authors. Wired said legal experts told it Judge Sidney H. Stein is not required to follow the filing, but would likely take it seriously because it comes from the Justice Department.

stories.headline: Nepal floods expose cross-border risk for India, especially Bihar and Uttar Pradesh
stories.dek: Nepal's floods are a warning for India because the two countries share river systems that rise in the Himalayas and flow into the Indian plains, the BBC reported.
stories.body:
Nepal’s floods are a warning for India because the two countries share river systems that rise in the Himalayas and flow into the Indian plains, the BBC reported. Nepal has more than 6,000 rivers and streams, most draining south into India and the Ganges. The BBC said seven to nine major rivers flow from Nepal into India, including the Kosi, Gandaki, Karnali and Mahakali, along with smaller rivers such as the Bagmati, Kamala, Rapti and Babai.

The BBC said Bihar is the Indian state most exposed, with roughly three-quarters of north Bihar officially classified as flood-prone. It said eastern Uttar Pradesh is also vulnerable, with districts including Gorakhpur, Bahraich, Lakhimpur Kheri and Shravasti regularly affected, while Uttarakhand shares the Mahakali-Sharda rivers and North Bengal receives the Mechi and Mahananda. “Bihar dominates in scale. Uttar Pradesh is second and often under-reported,” Pradeep Man Dangol of the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development told the BBC.

The BBC reported that hydrologists describe the danger as a three-part chain: where and how heavily rain falls in Nepal, how rivers drop sediment and spread across the plains, and what the water meets in India. Saswata Sanyal of ICIMOD told the BBC, “For the peak flow arriving at the border, largely Nepal’s rainfall; for the severity of flooding once it arrives, at least as much on Indian conditions.” The BBC cited the 2008 Kosi disaster in Bihar, when nearly 400 people died after an embankment in Nepal breached. Rajiv Sinha of IIT Kanpur told the BBC the river flow was only about a tenth of its carrying capacity and that the failure was due to embankments built in the 1950s and 1960s that had not been properly maintained.

India can get “roughly 12 hours to two days of warning” for ordinary monsoon floods, Sanyal told the BBC, though flash floods from Chure rivers can arrive within hours. The BBC said Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology shares rainfall and river-level data with India’s Central Water Commission, but quoted Sanyal as saying there are still too few real-time monitoring stations in the fastest-flowing catchments and no single shared forecasting model. In Nepal, the New York Times reported that people have been coming to photograph a green-painted “Miracle House” in Dhunge Bazaar after it kept the Pyakurel family safe while the surrounding area was destroyed by floodwaters.
stories.so_what: For readers in northern India, the report means flood danger can rise quickly across the border and the damage at home can hinge on local embankments, drainage and preparedness as much as on rain in Nepal.

Sannes wrote that the law operated in an area “in which the federal interest is so dominant that it cannot be enforced,” Inside Climate News reported. The New York Times also reported that the court said the measure conflicted with federal law.

Ken Lovett, a senior communications adviser on energy and environment for Hochul, said in an email to Inside Climate News that “taxpayers shouldn’t have to foot the bill for damages caused by polluters” and that the state is reviewing the decision. stories.dek: Rescue teams in Nepal are still trying to reach workers trapped in hydropower facilities more than a week after flash floods hit areas near the Nepal-China border.
stories.body:
Rescue teams in Nepal are still trying to reach workers trapped in hydropower facilities more than a week after flash floods hit areas near the Nepal-China border. Al Jazeera reported Thursday that more than 1,270 people had been killed and more than 4,700 were still missing. Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 1,252 bodies had been recovered in Nepal and 4,216 people were missing there, while Chinese authorities reported 21 deaths and 541 people missing in Tibet.

Earlier counts were lower. Euronews reported that on Tuesday Nepal's disaster agency had counted 987 deaths and 3,916 missing people, including 583 foreigners, and said Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 missing in their latest Sunday update. Euronews said at least 11,814 people had been rescued so far.

Both outlets said the 26 August disaster followed a collapse high in the Himalayas. Al Jazeera said scientists believe a glacier collapse near the Langtang Lirung mountain peak sent rocks, mud and water into valleys, while Euronews said scientists studying satellite imagery found a glacial collapse and bedrock failure beneath a glacier that registered as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.

The immediate focus is on hydropower sites in Nepal. Euronews said at least 900 workers were missing from 12 damaged hydropower projects and about 500 were believed trapped inside tunnels. Al Jazeera reported that hundreds of workers were believed trapped, including some in tunnels, and quoted Nepalese army engineering officer Sanjay Kc saying, "We still hope there are some survivors inside." He said one powerhouse was a big room and rescuers felt it was not fully flooded.

Authorities are also moving survivors and planning rebuilding. Al Jazeera said rescuers were using zip lines and helicopters to reach remote villages, and the UNDP estimated at least 2.2 million tonnes of debris. Dharma Raj Upreti, chief of the NDRRMA, told Reuters that about 20,000 houses would have to be rebuilt, including 7,500 destroyed, and said rebuilding in the same locations would expose people to the same risks.
stories.so_what: For people in Nepal and nearby areas, the disaster has destroyed homes, cut roads and bridges, and left thousands of families waiting for news of missing relatives.
stories.what_now: Prime Minister Balendra Shah said on Wednesday that authorities would continue searching for survivors while also starting rehabilitation and rebuilding efforts.

stories.headline: Met Office says summer 2026 was UK's hottest on record
stories.dek: Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data cited by the BBC, the Guardian and Sky News.
stories.body:
Summer 2026 was the UK's hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data cited by the BBC, the Guardian and Sky News. The Met Office said the average mean temperature across June, July and August was 16.5C, the warmest in a series going back to 1884.

The BBC said the summer brought five widespread heatwaves and 40 days with temperatures above 30C, breaking the previous record of 34 days set in 1995. It said 10 days reached 35C or higher, compared with the previous record of five, and three separate days reached 37C or higher, also a record. The highest temperature of the summer was 38.1C at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, according to the BBC and the Guardian.

England, Wales and Northern Ireland each set summer mean temperature records, while Scotland had its joint sixth warmest summer, the BBC and Guardian reported. The Guardian said this was the second year in a row that UK summer temperature records were broken, and that 1976 is now the seventh warmest summer by mean temperature.

In a rapid attribution study, the Met Office said the summer's average temperature was made about 130 times more likely by human-induced climate change. Dr Mark McCarthy, the Met Office's head of climate attribution, called the summer of 2026 "remarkable" and said it was "an example of the extremes we can expect to see more frequently as a consequence of human-induced climate change."
stories.so_what: The heat was linked in the sources to school closures, cancelled hospital appointments, drought, wildfires and flash flooding, affecting daily life across the UK.
stories.what_now: The Guardian reported that on Wednesday the Conservative party is due to present a 10-minute rule motion to parliament to repeal the Climate Change Act 2008.

stories.headline: US medical groups issue vaccine guidance for flu, COVID and RSV
stories.dek: A coalition of U.S. medical groups on Wednesday urged people to get updated vaccines for flu, COVID-19 and RSV, issuing its own guidance as federal advice has shifted or not been…
stories.body:
A coalition of U.S. medical groups on Wednesday urged people to get updated vaccines for flu, COVID-19 and RSV, issuing its own guidance as federal advice has shifted or not been updated. The groups include the American Medical Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

The groups said annual flu shots should be given to everyone ages six months and older. They also backed updated COVID-19 vaccines more broadly than current federal approvals, recommending them for healthy adults, young children and pregnant women. Al Jazeera reported the coalition also advised RSV immunisations for older adults, pregnant women and children younger than eight months. The Guardian reported family physicians recommend all adults get a COVID-19 vaccination, especially seniors and people with risk factors, while pediatricians recommend shots for children ages six months to 23 months and older children with high-risk conditions, and support vaccination for any child whose parent wants it.

"There's been a lot of confusion and chaos regarding vaccine recommendations," Dr Sandra Fryhofer of the AMA said, according to the Guardian. Al Jazeera quoted Fryhofer saying patients "need and deserve vaccine recommendations that are clear, credible, and based on the best available scientific evidence" and that the public needs "clear, consistent, science-based guidance even while the federal process is in flux."

The groups said recent studies show the shots continue to protect against severe illness, hospitalisation and death. Al Jazeera, citing CDC estimates for the 2025-2026 respiratory virus season, reported influenza caused about 32 million to 52 million cases, 390,000 hospitalisations and 24,000 deaths in the U.S.; COVID caused about 4.6 million to 12.9 million cases, 140,000 to 240,000 hospitalisations and 15,000 to 42,000 deaths; and RSV caused an estimated 2.8 million to 5.8 million outpatient visits, 170,000 to 340,000 hospitalisations, and up to 25,000 deaths.
stories.so_what: For patients and families deciding on fall shots, the guidance offers a nonfederal roadmap on who should be vaccinated as pharmacies and clinics begin offering updated doses.

stories.headline: Mental health A&E visits by children in England rise 36% since 2019
stories.dek: Children as young as six are going to A&E in England in mental health crisis in growing numbers, according to an analysis by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health…
stories.body:
Children as young as six are going to A&E in England in mental health crisis in growing numbers, according to an analysis by the Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health based on NHS England data obtained through the Freedom of Information Act. The college said attendances by six to 17-year-olds with a recorded mental health concern rose to 75,491 in 2025 from 55,525 in 2019, a 36% increase. The BBC said the overall rise in A&E attendances over the same period was just over 8%.

The sources said the biggest increases were among younger children. Medscape reported attendances rose by 62% among children aged six to nine and by 41% among those aged 9-15. The BBC also said some of the biggest rises were seen in children aged six to nine.

Long waits also increased. The BBC said more than 6,200 children and young people, around 8%, waited more than 12 hours in A&E in 2025. Medscape said the share waiting more than 12 hours more than doubled between 2019 and 2025, from around one in 29 to nearly one in 13, while the proportion waiting more than 24 hours rose by 320% and those staying more than three days rose by 514%.

Dr Sam Jones of the RCPCH said, according to the BBC, that "behind every one of these figures is a child or young person in distress and a family who didn't know where else to turn" and that emergency departments were "never designed" for children in mental health crisis to wait for days. The BBC quoted a Department of Health and Social Care spokesman saying, "No child should have to reach crisis point before getting the support they need," and said the government planned to publish a new mental health strategy later in the summer while expanding mental health teams in schools and more than 150 community mental health hubs.
stories.so_what: For families, the figures point to longer waits in unsuitable emergency departments when children cannot get help earlier in the community.
stories.what_now: The government is planning to publish a new mental health strategy later in the summer.

stories.headline: Ex-defence minister says MoD misled him on nuclear test veterans' records
stories.dek: Former defence minister Tobias Ellwood said the Ministry of Defence gave him incorrect information that led him to mislead parliament about medical records linked to British…
stories.body:
Former defence minister Tobias Ellwood said the Ministry of Defence gave him incorrect information that led him to mislead parliament about medical records linked to British nuclear bomb test veterans. Writing in the Guardian, Ellwood said that in December 2018 he told MPs the MoD was "unable to locate any information" showing blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring during the tests, but he now knows "the reality was very different".

Ellwood said blood samples were taken across the armed services branches, but veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses after radiation exposure have been unable to access them. He wrote: "This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed." The BBC reported that Cold War veterans who oversaw nuclear tests have claimed they caused lifelong health problems.

According to the Guardian, about 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale nuclear weapons tests in Australia and the South Pacific between 1952 and 1967. The paper said many later suffered blood disorders and cancers they believed were caused by radioactive fallout, and that most were denied pensions because of their ill health.

The Guardian said the government had long maintained it did not hold such medical records, but that claim was proved wrong in 2022 when journalist Susie Boniface revealed a classified database of 28,000 documents known as Merlin. Ellwood said he did not learn of the database until 2022 and asked: "If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture?"
stories.so_what: The admission adds pressure on the government to explain what records it held and could affect veterans' efforts to seek compensation for illnesses they link to the tests.

Two people were killed and the suspect was dead after a shooting at an apartment building in downtown Minneapolis on Wednesday afternoon, officials said.

Police said three officers were also taken to hospital. According to Parten, two of them were shot. A hospital spokesperson told AFP they were in "stable condition" and expected to survive. One officer was shot in the leg and another was in surgery, according to The Hindu's account of the press conference. It was not clear what injury the third officer sustained.

The police department and Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey warned people to stay away from the Loring Park neighborhood, the Guardian reported. Parten did not mention a motive at the press conference. Minnesota Governor Tim Walz wrote, "Minnesota is praying for our first responders" and asked the public to "pray for Minnesota." FBI Director Kash Patel said FBI agents were responding.

stories.headline: Maduro and wife ask US judge to throw out drug case on immunity
stories.dek: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, asked a judge on Wednesday to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them, arguing they have…
stories.body:
Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, asked a judge on Wednesday to dismiss the drug trafficking indictment against them, arguing they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country. In papers filed in Manhattan federal court, Maduro's lawyers wrote: "No American court has ever presided over the criminal trial of a foreign leader who was recognized by their own country as the sitting head of state at the time the charges were brought."

Flores filed a separate motion saying she also has sovereign immunity. Her lawyers wrote: "It is an attribute of Venezuela's sovereignty, and only Venezuela may surrender it." Maduro's lawyers also argued that even if he were not entitled to head-of-state immunity, the case must be dismissed because he has conduct-based sovereign immunity. They said he "vehemently denies the allegations against him" and was "falsely accused."

Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have pleaded not guilty in a criminal case first brought six years ago against numerous alleged co-conspirators. They have been held at a Brooklyn jail since U.S. forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid in early January and brought them to New York. President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid as a "surgical law enforcement operation," while Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.

U.S. prosecutors say Maduro helped carry out a conspiracy to move thousands of tons of cocaine into the U.S. by colluding with Venezuelan law enforcement to help drug kingpins. If convicted, Maduro and Flores face potential life prison sentences if a jury finds they were part of a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S.
stories.so_what: The immunity fight could decide whether the U.S. case reaches a jury at all in a prosecution that carries possible life sentences.
stories.what_now: Judge Alvin K. Hellerstein set oral arguments on the motions to dismiss for Nov. 17, and the trial is scheduled for June 1 next year.

stories.dek: Tiger Woods was given a five-year driving ban on Wednesday after changing his plea in Martin County, Florida, over a March rollover crash in Hobe Sound.
stories.body:
Tiger Woods was given a five-year driving ban on Wednesday after changing his plea in Martin County, Florida, over a March rollover crash in Hobe Sound. The 50-year-old agreed not to contest a reckless driving charge, according to the Guardian and BBC, while CBS Sports reported he amended his plea to guilty. He was fined $1,000 for reckless driving and $500 for refusing to submit to a lawful test, and court records cited by the Guardian show he paid $2,131.44 in fines and costs.

Prosecutors had originally charged Woods with driving under the influence with property damage. Authorities said he passed a breath test showing no alcohol, but refused a urine test. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Woods was driving a Land Rover that overturned after he tried to overtake a truck on a narrow two-lane road shortly before 2pm on 27 March. Investigators said he showed signs of impairment. BBC reported police later found two white pills in his pocket identified as hydrocodone.

The Guardian reported Woods told investigators he had taken several medications earlier that day, including drugs for high blood pressure and cholesterol, ibuprofen and Vicodin. Body camera footage released in April, cited by the BBC, showed Woods saying, "I looked down at my phone, and all of a sudden, boom". No one was injured, and Woods was able to get out through the passenger side of the vehicle.

Florida State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl said after the hearing, "I'm completely confident and comfortable with the resolution of this case." He added: "Today I resolved case involving a man who drives a golf ball for a living. Tomorrow, I'll resolve a case in the same matter for a man who drives a nail for a living." The Guardian said Woods also agreed not to seek a hardship exemption during the suspension and did not answer reporters' questions as he arrived and left court with Vanessa Trump.
stories.so_what: The deal closes the criminal case from the March crash and keeps Woods off the road for five years while he remains away from competition seeking treatment.

stories.headline: Judge blocks Trump’s new order limiting birthright citizenship
stories.dek: A federal judge in Maryland on Wednesday blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order that sought to limit who qualifies for birthright citizenship.
stories.body:
A federal judge in Maryland on Wednesday blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order that sought to limit who qualifies for birthright citizenship. U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman issued a preliminary injunction after two immigration advocacy groups challenged the order.

Euronews reported that Boardman said the Supreme Court had already settled the issue. “The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” she wrote in a 35-page ruling. The New York Times said the ruling raised concerns that babies already defined as citizens by the Supreme Court could have their citizenship revoked under the August order.

Trump signed the order on 6 August. Euronews said it targeted what Trump termed “birth tourism,” people he alleges enter the country as tourists while intending to give birth. It was his second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship after lower courts, and then the Supreme Court, blocked an earlier order that said children born to parents in the United States illegally or on temporary visas would not automatically become U.S. citizens.

Administration lawyers argued that a court order was premature because agencies had not yet issued guidance on how they would enforce the measure, according to Euronews. Boardman rejected that argument, writing: “No matter what the guidance says, the 2026 Executive Order commands agencies to deny citizenship documents to several broad categories of children.” Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, said, “When it comes to attacking birthright citizenship, the Trump administration has lost before this court, lost before the Supreme Court, and lost again today.”
stories.so_what: The decision keeps the government from denying citizenship documents while the case moves forward, preserving the status of children born in the United States who would be affected by the order.

stories.headline: Malta jury acquits Yorgen Fenech over Daphne Caruana Galizia murder
stories.dek: A Maltese jury has found businessman Yorgen Fenech, 44, not guilty of involvement in the murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
stories.body:
A Maltese jury has found businessman Yorgen Fenech, 44, not guilty of involvement in the murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. The verdict was delivered at 7.30pm on Wednesday, with the forewoman saying jurors voted by an 8-1 majority to dismiss both charges: complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, and association with the intention of committing a crime.

The Guardian reported the prosecution is expected to appeal. Prosecutors had accused Fenech of paying €150,000 via middleman Melvin Theuma to have Caruana Galizia killed in October 2017. Fenech denied ordering the killing, telling the jury: "I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia's murder, or anyone else's. I had no role in her murder."

The acquittal drew gasps in court and cheers from Fenech's relatives, according to The Guardian. Caruana Galizia's sister, Corinne Vella, said: "Everybody is much more at risk now, because this signals you can kill journalists with impunity." Her eldest son said on Facebook it was a "terrible decision by the jurors that our country may never recover from".

The case has become a major press freedom and anti-corruption issue in Malta. The government said it noted the verdict and appealed for prudence in public comments, adding: "The government remains committed to seeing justice served by its institutions." Opposition leader Alex Borg called for parliament to be urgently reopened to discuss the verdict, while campaign groups Repubblika and Occupy Justice said full accountability had still not been reached.

stories.dek: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security, in his second prosecution…
stories.body:
Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security, in his second prosecution under Beijing's 2020 national security law. Euronews and the Guardian said Wong, 29, entered the plea at Hong Kong's high court. Sky News said the charge could see him sentenced to life in prison.

Prosecutors said Wong worked with exiled activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against Hong Kong and China. Euronews reported prosecutors alleged Wong supported efforts from Hong Kong through foreign and social media, including sharing Law's posts and an online petition urging digital forensic companies to stop cooperating with police. The New York Times said Wong was accused of urging Western politicians including Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio to pressure Hong Kong by imposing sanctions on the city.

Wong is already serving four years and eight months after pleading guilty in a separate national security case linked to an unofficial political primary, according to Euronews. The Guardian said he has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020, has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027. Euronews said that before his arrest in this case in June 2025, he had been expected to be freed next January.

Euronews and the Guardian said the offence is punishable by three to 10 years in prison, or up to life imprisonment if it is deemed "of a grave nature," and that a guilty plea could typically reduce the sentence. The Guardian reported Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock, while Euronews said a supporter shouted, "Hang in there" before the hearing and people queued overnight to get seats.
stories.so_what: The plea means one of Hong Kong's best-known democracy activists is likely to stay in prison beyond his previously expected release date.

stories.headline: Judge sends Tyler Robinson to trial in Charlie Kirk killing case
stories.dek: A Utah judge on Tuesday sent Tyler Robinson to trial in the 2025 killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and allowed prosecutors to keep an aggravated murder charge that…
stories.body:
A Utah judge on Tuesday sent Tyler Robinson to trial in the 2025 killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and allowed prosecutors to keep an aggravated murder charge that makes Robinson eligible for the death penalty. Utah District Judge Tony Graf ruled after a preliminary hearing in Provo, Utah. One of Robinson's lawyers then entered a not-guilty plea on his behalf, while Euronews reported Robinson pleaded not guilty to all counts.

Prosecutors said Robinson, 23, shot Kirk once in the neck from a rooftop more than 400 feet, or 122 meters, away as Kirk spoke at an open-air event at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah, before a crowd that Euronews said was more than 3,000 people. Prosecutor Ryan McBride said there was a "mountain of evidence," including DNA, messages with Robinson's romantic partner and posts on Discord. Prosecutors also cited a handwritten note they allege Robinson left saying, "I had the opportunity to take out Charlie Kirk, and I took it."

Robinson's lawyers tried to stop the case from going to trial or at least remove the death penalty from consideration. Defense lawyer Staci Visser said prosecutors were trying to "shoehorn" the case into Utah's aggravated murder law and had shown only a possibility, not a high probability, that others could have been killed. "There is one shot. There is one bullet. There is one victim," Visser said. "There is zero evidence that there was any action taken towards other people."

Graf said the aggravated murder charge was supported by "the documented position of several individuals in and around the canopy area" where Kirk was speaking. Euronews reported he also cited the positions of several people in and around a tent. Prosecutor Chad Grunander said the alleged murder weapon, a bolt-action rifle, was loaded with additional rounds and that Robinson "came prepared to shoot again."

Kirk's family called the ruling "an important step in our family's pursuit of justice." In a statement, they said, "Every step in this process carries the weight of all that Charlie's murder has taken from his family, especially his children who will grow up without their father." Prosecutors are also seeking sentencing enhancements by arguing Robinson targeted Kirk for his political beliefs, citing an engraved bullet reading, "Hey Fascist! CATCH!" and a text they allege Robinson wrote: "I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can't be negotiated out."
stories.so_what: The ruling means the case will move toward a full trial with the possibility of capital punishment still in play.

stories.dek: A jury in Las Vegas found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur, ending a case that had remained unresolved for close to 30 years.
stories.body:
A jury in Las Vegas found Duane "Keffe D" Davis guilty of orchestrating the 1996 killing of Tupac Shakur, ending a case that had remained unresolved for close to 30 years. Euronews said the jury deliberated for less than three hours after a nine-day trial. The New York Times said Davis, 63, was convicted after he went on an interview tour discussing his role in the drive-by shooting.

The sources differ on how the conviction was described. Euronews reported Davis was convicted on a single count of murder with a deadly weapon, while the BBC said he was charged with murder with a deadly weapon. The New York Times said he was found guilty of first-degree murder.

Prosecutors said Davis acquired a gun and "went hunting" for Shakur and Marion "Suge" Knight after his nephew was beaten earlier that night, according to Euronews. Prosecutors also said Davis repeatedly placed himself inside the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired, and argued that although he did not pull the trigger, he called for the gunfire. Defence attorney Michael Sanft said there was no physical evidence tying Davis to the shooting and argued his public statements and the memoir "Compton Street Legend" were dramatized bravado meant to make money.

Shakur was shot multiple times in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996 and died six days later, the BBC and Euronews reported. Euronews said Shakur's sister, Sekyiwa "Set" Shakur, cried and hugged prosecutors after the verdict, while Davis' son covered his face with one hand. The New York Times reported that even after the conviction, some people close to Shakur still say questions remain.
stories.so_what: The verdict closes one of the longest-running unsolved cases in popular music, but the differing accounts and remaining questions mean some people still do not see it as full closure.
stories.what_now: Sentencing is scheduled for October, and Euronews reported Davis is expected to appeal the conviction.

stories.headline: NBA fines Clippers $30 million and strips five picks over Kawhi Leonard probe
stories.dek: The NBA said Wednesday that it fined the Los Angeles Clippers $30 million and took away five first-round draft picks after an investigation found salary cap circumvention tied to…
stories.body:
The NBA said Wednesday that it fined the Los Angeles Clippers $30 million and took away five first-round draft picks after an investigation found salary cap circumvention tied to Kawhi Leonard. The league said the Clippers will forfeit one first-round pick in each draft from 2029 through 2033. It also said the team and its personnel will be placed under a league-run compliance and monitoring program for five years.

The NBA suspended owner Steve Ballmer from all league and team activities for one year. It also suspended president of business operations Gillian Zucker for one year without pay and president of basketball operations Lawrence Frank for six months without pay. The league fined Leonard $700,000 and banned his uncle and former business manager, Dennis Robertson, from doing business with NBA teams and affiliates for five years.

According to the NBA and a Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz report cited by several outlets, the Clippers initiated off-court income opportunities between Leonard and four companies that did business with the team: Aspiration Partners, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics and Lockton Insurance. The league said the team facilitated endorsement deals, induced companies to enter them by offering team business, paid personal expenses for Leonard and his representatives, and failed to report improper solicitations made on Leonard's behalf. The NBA said Ballmer knowingly sought to help Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities and approved a deal he knew was a precondition for Aspiration to sign an endorsement agreement with Leonard.

Commissioner Adam Silver said he was "deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct." The Clippers said, "We vehemently reject the NBA's findings," calling the investigation "heavily biased" and saying they would fight the penalties "through every avenue available to us" in an "ethical and impartial arbitration process." Leonard said he accepted "full responsibility for lapses in judgment by people within my inner circle" but said he entered the contract and agreements "in good faith" and had "no knowledge of any intent on anyone's part to circumvent the salary cap."
stories.so_what: The punishment hits the Clippers on several fronts at once, taking away future draft assets, removing top executives from their jobs and leaving the team under league oversight for five years.
stories.what_now: Several outlets said Leonard's agreed trade to the Toronto Raptors, which had been on hold pending the investigation, can now move toward completion.

Chelsea reached the Women’s Champions League league phase with a 1-0 win at Real Sociedad on Wednesday, sealing a 6-2 aggregate victory in their third qualifying round tie. Keira Walsh scored the only goal in the 54th minute at Instalaciones de Zubieta in San Sebastián.

Sonia Bompastor made four changes, with Lucy Bronze, Kadiesha Buchanan, Lexi Potter and Wieke Kaptein starting, according to Sky Sports. The Guardian said Walsh swept in from a corner in the 54th minute.

Real Sociedad, now under Gorka Álvarez after Arturo Ruiz left and was unveiled as Brighton manager between the two legs, held Chelsea at bay for long spells but could not revive the tie. Hannah Hampton saved from Ainhoa Marin during a brief home spell, while Chelsea gave debuts off the bench to Nelly Las and Giulia Dragoni, according to the Guardian. Bompastor said: "I'm pleased with the result. We kept a clean sheet, which is always important," and added: "The goal was for us to qualify, which is what we have done."

stories.headline: Grammy-winning jazz singer Cassandra Wilson dies at 70
stories.dek: Cassandra Wilson, the two-time Grammy-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer, died Wednesday at 70.
stories.body:
Cassandra Wilson, the two-time Grammy-winning jazz singer, songwriter and producer, died Wednesday at 70. Her manager, Robert Torre, told New Jersey radio station WBGO that Wilson “transitioned peacefully at home, surrounded by family, close friends, and her manager.” Rolling Stone said no cause of death was cited.

Born on Dec. 4, 1955, in Jackson, Mississippi, Wilson grew up in a musical family and later earned a degree in mass communications from Jackson State University, according to Rolling Stone. The New York Times said her low, smoky voice drew on the blues tradition of her native Mississippi, while the Guardian said her idiosyncratic contralto helped her move across folk, pop, R&B, country and beyond.

After moving to New York in 1982, Wilson co-founded the M-Base Collective with saxophonist Steve Coleman, Rolling Stone reported. “From Steve Coleman, I learned to tear a piece of music apart and get away from standard approaches,” Wilson told Time in 2001, according to Rolling Stone. She released her debut solo album, Point of View, in 1986, and later made Blue Light ’til Dawn, New Moon Daughter, Traveling Miles, Loverly and Coming Forth by Day, her final solo album in 2015.

Wilson also worked with a wide range of artists, including the Roots, Angélique Kidjo, Wynton Marsalis, Greg Osby, Terence Blanchard, Elvis Costello, Meshell Ndegeocello and Luther Vandross, Rolling Stone reported. She told The New York Times in 1994, according to Rolling Stone, “I continue to choose the path I take musically. And it’s not motivated by becoming famous or having a lot money, or any other pop motivation.”
stories.so_what: Her death closes the career of a singer whose recordings and collaborations reached well beyond jazz, touching listeners across several styles of American music.

stories.headline: King Charles and Macron open Bayeux Tapestry display at British Museum
stories.dek: King Charles III visited the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum in London on Wednesday with French President Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
stories.body:
King Charles III visited the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum in London on Wednesday with French President Emmanuel Macron and Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Charles called the loan "the best possible symbol" of the "entente amicale" between France and the UK and said the tapestry was now "a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations."

The tapestry, an embroidered account of the Norman conquest, is about 70 meters long and is on loan from France until September 2027, the Guardian reported. DW said it is on loan for a 10-month exhibition opening next week, on September 10. Both outlets said it is the first time the work has been on British soil since the 11th century.

Macron said the return of the tapestry "had required a little patience" since he first spoke of it in 2018. Referring to a British request dating back to 1931, he said: "I choose to regard eight years as something of a speed record." He added that he hoped the two countries could "forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery."

Burnham called the loan "a great example of French-British cooperation" and said in parliament that the same cooperation had helped reduce summer small boat crossings "to a seven-year low." The Guardian said Britain will lend the Sutton Hoo treasures, a selection of Lewis chess pieces and other British Museum objects to museums in France in return, while Burnham also promoted a Bayeux Around Britain digital exhibition for venues across the UK.

The visit also included Queen Camilla, Brigitte Macron and Burnham's wife, Marie-France van Heel. The party stopped at scenes including the coronation of Harold Godwinson and the depiction of his death at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, according to the Guardian. The New York Times said Charles saw the embroidery almost 40 years after viewing it in France with Diana.
stories.so_what: The loan and exchange of major artefacts turn a diplomatic gesture into something the public in Britain and France will be able to see in museums.
stories.what_now: The British Museum exhibition opens to the public on September 10.

stories.headline: Met cancels John Galliano exhibit tied to 2027 Met Gala after backlash
stories.dek: The Metropolitan Museum of Art said Monday it is canceling its planned spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition on British designer John Galliano, which had been set to launch…
stories.body:
The Metropolitan Museum of Art said Monday it is canceling its planned spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition on British designer John Galliano, which had been set to launch with the 2027 Met Gala. The museum said the show, announced as "John Galliano: Horizons," will be replaced by another exhibit. NPR also reported that Galliano will no longer be celebrated at the 2027 gala, while Sky News said the 2027 Met Gala honouring his career had been cancelled.

Met director and CEO Max Hollein said, "Following thoughtful discussions with John Galliano, we have together decided not to proceed with the exhibition." Galliano said on social media and in the museum statement that after "much reflection and discussion" he had decided "with great sadness" that the exhibition should not take place now. He said he remains "fully accountable" for the pain caused by his past words, "particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities."

The planned show drew weeks of backlash because of Galliano's antisemitic and racist comments in 2010 and 2011. NPR reported he was fired by Christian Dior after the remarks surfaced and was convicted in an antisemitism trial in France. Among the comments cited by NPR were "I love Hitler" and a statement to Jewish patrons that their mothers and forefathers would have been "gassed." CBS said the remarks led to his dismissal from Dior and a hate crime conviction in France.

Anna Wintour said Galliano's decision was "very courageous" and "the right decision." Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute curator, said he believes museums must examine difficult histories with "rigor, candor, and care" but also recognized "the pain and concern this exhibition has caused." New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin, a prominent critic of the plan, said the exhibit had been "a gut punch to the Jewish community" and called the cancellation "the correct decision."

CBS, citing The New York Times, reported that donors had threatened to rescind gifts if the museum moved ahead. NPR reported the gala traditionally takes place on the first Monday in May, which in 2027 falls on Holocaust Remembrance Day, and said there had been speculation the museum might change the date for that reason.

stories.what_now: The Met said it will announce details on a new spring Costume Institute exhibition and the 2027 Met Gala at a later date.
